newsitem.title: USA: NYS Gov. says welfare issues complicate budget.
newsitem.headline: NYS Gov. says welfare issues complicate budget.

text.p: New York State Gov. George Pataki, whose budget this summer set a national record for lateness, on Tuesday said that the thorny issue of welfare reform could make it hard for him to submit a budget in December.

New York is one of the states that is expected to get hit particularly hard under the new federal plan because its constitution obliges it to care for the needy and it has one of the nation's biggest, most costly welfare programs.

While a number of states already have submitted their plans to the federal government, which qualifies them to collect bonuses for filing early, New York's task force still is examining how best to adjust its programs.
The group, whose work was delayed by the new law's complexity, expects to hold its last meeting in mid- to late October, and give the governor its recommendations a short time later.

Pataki told reporters in Albany that he aims to call a special session of the legislature in December, with the hope of finishing as much of the "welfare debate" as possible before the new session starts in January.

"It's going to be very difficult to do a December budget, we have the federal welfare reform and I'm hopeful that in December we can make some progress toward changing our laws to comply with federal laws."
New York's budget is due April 1.
One of the problems New York State faces is that unlike a number of other states, it matches new federal laws with its own.
It is not yet clear whether the state can submit its plan to Washington until the end of a 45-day comment period and until the legislature has agreed on new welfare laws.

"We are still trying to see if we can do that," said John Signor, a spokesman for the state Budget Division. He added he understood that California was grappling with the same issue, and that if it went ahead and filed its plan and the federal government did not reject it, New York then would have a better feel for what Washington will allow.
How quickly New York can submit its plan is an importatnt issue because it stands to capture around $20 million for every month by which it beats the July 1 deadline.

Further, Pataki's plans to impose workfare requirements and set time limits stalled in the Assembly last year, which raises the possibility of another deadlock. "Just because there will be a special session doesn't have any bearing on whether there will be a conclusion," said Rus Sykes, deputy director of the State Community Aid Association in Albany.

The state's failure to develop a plan since the federal s bill was signed in late August likely will be criticized when the New York City Council holds a hearing on Wednesday on the fiscal impact of the new federal welfare bill.
"One thing that we're going to try to bring forward is a real call for the state to come up with innovative ideas. They haven't put anything out," said a Council spokesman.

The new welfare bill starts restricting benefits to legal immigrants next spring, and Mayor Rudolph Giuliani has said he plans to sue the federal government over sme of the new rules. He has estimated there are 400,000 legal and illegal aliens, who do not collect welfare but attend public schools and use public health facilities, in the city.
The state expects to be able to maximize its $2.4 billion block grant once it submits its plan.

And part of the new federal bill, the Temporary Assistance to Needy Families programs, could produce a surplus of $250 million to $300 million in the first year. But finance officials have said there are bigger risks in the program's later years even if some of the early issues might focus on questions like who will be eligible for the programs.

And welfare advocates have suggested that the state might want to ask Washington to waive workfare requirements for Food Stamps, which is paid for entirely by federal dollars, as such recipients might see their cash benefits cut.
